finding.claim: PUT /doc/<doc_id> overwrites the body of any document for any authenticated user. The edit-permission check is computed and discarded, so it never blocks the write.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled doc_id path parameter (docs.py:17) and request.json["body"] (docs.py:20). Precondition: the attacker can reach the route with some g.user value, including a user who is not an owner or editor. Authentication is set outside this file and is not visible here.
finding.sink: doc["body"] = request.json["body"] at docs.py:20, an unconditional write to document content.

trace.note: update_doc(doc_id) handles PUT /doc/<doc_id> with no authorization decorator.
doc = DOCS[doc_id] loads any document by ID with no ownership filter.
can_edit(g.user, doc) is called but its boolean result is not checked, so nothing aborts.
The request body is written into the document unconditionally.
Returns ok=True, so the unauthorized write succeeds silently.

finding.guards_checked: can_edit (docs.py:7-8) returns the correct owner-or-editor result, but its return value is discarded at line 19. There is no abort(403) on this path, no login_required or similar decorator in this file, and no check on g.user itself. The sibling route update_title (docs.py:24-29) calls require_edit at line 27, which aborts with 403, so the title endpoint is protected and the body endpoint is not.

verdict.guard_found: can_edit (docs.py:7-8) computes the correct owner-or-editor result, but line 19 calls it as a bare statement and discards the bool, so nothing aborts. require_edit (docs.py:11-13) would abort(403), but it is not called on the body path. No decorator, before_request hook, or ownership check on update_doc (docs.py:16-21) exists in this file. The only control is the sibling update_title route, which calls require_edit at docs.py:27.
verdict.reason: The handler at docs.py:17-21 loads any document by ID (line 18) and writes request.json["body"] (line 20) after a bare can_edit(g.user, doc) call at line 19 whose result is never tested, so any authenticated user with a valid g.user can overwrite any body; the title route at docs.py:27 uses require_edit and aborts, which shows the intended check was missed here.

finding.claim: An unknown doc_id raises an unhandled KeyError, which Flask turns into a 500. This is low-severity information leakage and a minor availability issue, not an authorization bypass.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled doc_id path parameter (docs.py:17), in update_doc or update_title.
finding.sink: DOCS[doc_id] dict lookup at docs.py:18 and docs.py:26. An uncaught exception returns a 500, and with debug mode enabled it can expose a traceback.

trace.note: doc_id comes directly from the URL.
DOCS[doc_id] raises KeyError when the ID is missing.

finding.guards_checked: No existence check and no DOCS.get() returning 404. The dict lookup is not an injection sink. Whether debug mode is enabled is not visible in this file.

verdict.guard_found: none. There is no existence check or DOCS.get() 404 path at docs.py:18 or docs.py:26. The only checks come after the lookup: can_edit/require_edit at docs.py:19 and docs.py:27. Those run only after DOCS[doc_id] has already succeeded.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: doc_id comes from the URL (docs.py:17), and DOCS[doc_id] at docs.py:18 and docs.py:26 raises an uncaught KeyError for an unknown ID before any permission check runs, so the request becomes a 500. The attacker can be anonymous, since the lookup precedes all authorization logic. Impact is low: it is an existence oracle (unknown IDs 500, known IDs return 403 to non-editors) plus availability noise, and the traceback exposure depends on debug mode, which this file does not show. Separately, docs.py:19 calls can_edit() as a bare statement and discards its bool, so update_doc (PUT /doc/<id>) has no authorization at all. That is a real, more serious authorization bypass, but it is not what DOC-2 claims, so it should be reported as its own finding.
